title: Your "personality" is just your 2yo attention hack
summary:
The most quotable gut-punch came from @eigenrobot: your core “personality” is basically “the series of tricks you used to get your parents’ attention when you were two”… a survival mechanism so load-bearing you never dropped it, you just “lacquered it” until it looked like a whole identity. That framing hit because it turns adult quirks into a forensic trace: not “who you are,” but what worked on your original audience.

The thread’s arc is: theory → receipts → application. @PrinceVogel tried to soften the determinism (“maybe 50% true”), arguing origins aren’t outcomes and those “tricks” keep evolving through contact with the world—also, they were how you connected with “the first people you loved,” which is kind of beautiful. Then @AskYatharth showed up with somatic proof: yoga makes it “very obvious” his personality is like “3 strategies” learned at age 2, and what’s spooky is realizing there’s a whole other set of impulses waiting when you stop pushing those buttons. Meanwhile @loopholekid stitched in the Alice Miller / “as-if personality” canon: kids self-obliterate to meet a parent’s emotional needs, repress feelings into the body, and grow up performing a false self—then dropped the nastiest mirror: “compulsive illegibility” on Twitter as a perfected version of that performance.

What made it peak was @eigenrobot turning it into a parenting live-demo: he watched his daughter run “continuous experiments” to get “attention of different flavors” (because if parents don’t attend, “they can literally die”), and he’s trying to reward playful theater while discouraging “HORRID WHINING”—aka shaping which attention-strategy becomes her default adult coating. The vibe later resolves into self-parenting: @AskYatharth’s takeaway is that for insecurely attached people, nothing beats “the parenting from your own inner adult.” Then the backlash note lands in 2025: @vividvoid warns about the “cult of the inner child,” where feeling your feelings tips into becoming too sensuous to keep commitments or do serious work.

Why care: it’s a sneaky diagnostic for why you keep doing the same weird, self-sabotaging thing in relationships/work—and it reframes “self-improvement” as not polishing the lacquer, but noticing the original attention trick, choosing when to retire it, and not turning inner-child work into another personality costume.
